newsitem.title: UK: UK retail sales waning ahead of election - analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK retail sales waning ahead of election - analysts.

text.p: British retail sales growth is running out of energy after bounding ahead late last year and analysts say anxiety about the up-coming general election may be the explanation.

Their comments followed data Confederation of British Industry data on Thursday which said sales growth in the three months to February was the lowest since May 1996 whilst sales in February itself had failed to live up to shopkeepers forecasts.
But both the CBI and analysts were keen to emphasise that consumers are merely taking a break.

"I don't think we're going to see weak sales throughout the year, it's more of a consolidation," CIBC chief economist David Coleman said. "With the election on its way, there's a good argument for caution."

Britain's ruling Conservative Party is widely expected to hold a general election on May 1 and consumers may be curbing their spending urges in case a new government, of whichever party, means either higher interest rates or higher taxes.
Morgan Stanley UK economist Kevin Gardiner said the CBI data suggested annual growth of only 2.5 percent in official retail sales compared with the 3.0 to 3.5 he had been expecting.
Gardiner said he would be downgrading his retail sales forecast. "My biggest worry is the impending election. Political uncertainty can have an impact on consumer sentiment," he said.

British financial markets took the view that the data represented a further vindication of Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's recent refusals to increase Britain's 6.0 percent interest rates.
"The CBI survey supports the Chancellor's view that there is no need for an early tightening in monetary policy," said one senior trader of UK government bonds.

"Not only are sales volumes disappointing, but also price pressures are clearly suppressed," he said. The data also showed the smallest annual increase in prices since August 1995 and that retailers expected similarly low increases in March.

Analysts said the combination of low price pressures and weaker consumer activity should go some way to allaying Bank of England Governor Eddie George's worries inflation will regain its grip on the economy if interest rates do not go up soon.
"There's nothing in these figures to justify a rate rise," NatWest Markets UK economist John O'Sullivan said.
"There's nothing to show consumer spending is picking up nor is it likely to until the Autumn, once we start seeing some of the windfall payments," O'Sullivan said.
Many British consumers are likely to receive hefty payments from mergers and flotations of building societies.
